## Before the first public release

*Condition:* `preparing_first_release or released`

### Needs you (19)

**SEC-16** · MUST · Release-signing keys live in a hardware token or KMS, not in a CI secret readable by build steps or on a download server. Custody is documented (who holds them, where, how), with an offline backup held by a second trusted person under LIFE-02, an expiry and rotation schedule, and a published revocation path.\
*Why:* A key readable by build steps is a key any compromised dependency can use. · *Checked in review.*

**A11Y-05** · MUST · Releases are tested with Orca, NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack on their Tier 1 platforms, and under the KDE protocol: keyboard only, pointer and on-screen keyboard only, touch only, an unfamiliar color scheme, a large system font, speakers muted, and animations disabled.\
*Why:* Automated checks miss what only a real assistive-technology session reveals. · *Checked before each release.*

**I18N-12** · MUST · Shipped translations are reviewed by a human; machine suggestions are never released unreviewed, and the English source is always complete. Each language has a named coordinator or team who reviews new translators' suggestions and keeps a per-language glossary seeded from the suite glossary. The first shipped languages are chosen by ADR.\
*Why:* Unreviewed machine output ships errors to users who cannot tell them from the source. · *Checked before each release.*

**UX-08** · MUST · Interfaces follow the suite's interface guidelines. The guidelines follow the common skeleton (principles, foundations, patterns, components, inputs, platforms, brand, reference), carry a dated change log on every page, and are owned by the module named in GOVERNANCE.md (GOV-07). Where they are silent, the host platform's guidelines apply. Details: interface guidelines.\
*Why:* A named owner and a change log keep the guidelines current, and a fallback covers what they omit. · *Checked in review.*\
*Open decision:* Interface guidelines. Leaning: Write them alongside the first app.

**UX-24** · MUST · Changes to shared components, tokens, interaction patterns or terminology need approval from the design owner (GOV-07). UI pull requests include before-and-after screenshots or a recording. New interaction patterns are validated by use-case analysis or user testing before they enter the component library (UX-02).\
*Why:* Shared UI changes reach every app; a named owner and visual evidence catch drift. · *Checked in review.*

**BRAND-04** · MUST · Every app's logo is composed on the logo skeleton: a construction grid of three equal circles whose centers form an upward equilateral triangle, separated by 0.3 to 0.5 times their radius, the exact ratio set by ADR after design review. A logo places its main forms on the grid without having to show the circles, and its silhouette differs from every other app's. Each logo ships full-color, monochrome (symbolic) and dark variants, a distinct pre-release variant, and icons fitting each platform's container and grid; at 32 px and below it uses simplified filled forms. The Flathub presentation ADR (UX-03) decides whether the skeleton can produce GNOME- and KDE-style icons.\
*Why:* Tinted, clear and symbolic icon modes strip color, so only distinct silhouettes tell apps apart at small sizes. · *Checked in review.*\
*Open decision:* Logo design review: the skeleton's gap ratio, the organization's mark, GNOME- and KDE-style icons. Leaning: none yet.

**PERF-06** · MUST · Each app publishes minimum hardware requirements (CPU, RAM, storage) and is tested each release on a reference machine at least five years old.\
*Why:* Blue Angel DE-UZ 215 ties efficiency to old hardware, which users keep for years. · *Checked before each release.*

**PLAT-09** · MUST · Windows and macOS builds are code-signed, macOS builds are notarized, and CI verifies both.\
*Why:* The Microsoft Store requires signing, and Gatekeeper blocks unnotarized macOS binaries. · *Enforced by CI.*

**PLAT-18** · MUST · Minimum OS versions per platform follow a written policy (for example, supported while the vendor supports them), rise only at the start of a release cycle, and meet each store's current target (Play requires API 36 for updates since 31 August 2026).\
*Why:* Stores refuse updates below their target level, and a mid-cycle rise strands users without notice. · *Checked in review.*

**DOC-14** · SHOULD · A public roadmap states current priorities per area and what the project will and will not do over the next year, without promised feature dates.\
*Why:* Priorities without dates tell contributors where help lands and avoid deadlines that slip. · *Checked in review.*

**REL-09** · MUST · Each project publishes a support policy and table, updated every release: which versions get fixes, for how long, and when security updates end. The current release is supported until the next release's first patch, and only the latest patch of a series is supported. LTS is deferred until 1.0. SECURITY.md links the table.\
*Why:* Users and reporters need to know which version to run and which versions get security fixes. · *Checked before each release.*

**REL-10** · MUST · Each app publishes a time-based target cadence (for example two releases a year) and an app version scheme. Target dates may slip. A release branch is cut before each release, followed by release candidates at least weekly, with a stated target date. Crates release when ready. Details: release-process document.\
*Why:* A rhythm gives users and translators dates to plan around; dates that slip avoid crunch. · *Checked before each release.*

**REL-13** · MUST · Every release has curated, plain-language notes for users, shipped in the AppStream release entry and kept separate from the generated changelog (REL-03), which is an input, never the notes. They cover what changed and the upgrade impact; a compatibility section (breaking changes, migrations, dropped platforms); every fixed vulnerability with its advisory or CVE ID; and any change to data collection or contacted servers. A cumulative compatibility page is kept.\
*Why:* Users decide whether to upgrade from the notes; a commit list doesn't tell them. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-04** · MUST · The trademark policy lists uses allowed without asking (*made with Kreqo*, plugins and decks *for Kreqo*, tutorials, non-profit events), offers a community badge, reserves the logo, and defines an extension namespace such as `kreqo-ext-`. Third-party product names never begin with Kreqo, forks rebrand, the plugin directory refuses listings that misuse the marks, and the marks pass to the next maintainers if the project is abandoned.\
*Why:* Listed permitted uses stop the community asking for every badge or tutorial. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-05** · MUST · Personal data handling complies with Quebec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector as modernized by Law 25, with PIPEDA (or its successor once in force) for interprovincial and international flows and the GDPR for EU users. Hosted services offered to people in the EU designate an EU representative (GDPR Art. 27) before launch, unless an ADR documents why the exemption applies.\
*Why:* Law 25 reaches any enterprise handling Quebec residents' data; a sync service is not occasional processing under the GDPR. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-10** · MUST · Before the first release containing cryptography, an export-control ADR per app records its status under the Canadian Export Control List (software in the public domain), the US EAR (publicly available, standard cryptography only) and each store's answers (Apple's encryption flag and the French declaration). Source is public before or with every binary.\
*Why:* Every download is an export transfer; public source using standard cryptography needs no permit. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-12** · MUST · A Canadian trademark application for the word mark KREQO (downloadable software and online services) is filed before the first release and extended through the Madrid Protocol to the EU and US before commercial use. App names, "Kreqo" plus a plain word (BRAND-02), are covered by that mark.\
*Why:* Canada has required no proof of use since 2019, so anyone can file first. · *Checked before each release.*

**LIFE-03** · MUST · GOVERNANCE.md names at least two maintainers or states the bus-factor risk; every maintainer role has a named backup and a runbook; the founder's role has a written handover plan.\
*Why:* A runbook turns a crisis handover into a procedure. · *Checked in review.*

**LIFE-05** · MUST · A project becomes stable only after a public admission review: an issue holding the admission checklist (every Release-check rule plus licensing, metadata, translations and packaging) stays open at least 14 days with evidence for each item; a review still failing after 60 days returns the project to incubating.\
*Why:* A public checklist with evidence is what the Kreqo name promises. · *Checked before each release.*

## Before the first Android release

*Condition:* `android_release`

### Needs you (1)

**PLAT-17** · MUST · An ADR decides the response to Android developer verification (register or not, how F-Droid users install and update, how package names are protected), and is revisited when Google's global rollout starts in 2027.\
*Why:* Verification decides whether F-Droid users can install the app at all, and package names can be claimed by others. · *Checked in review.*

### Checked for you (1)

- **PLAT-16** · SHOULD · Android builds are reproducible and signed with one organization key across F-Droid (developer-signed publishing), Play and direct download, so users can switch channels without reinstalling. *(tooling)*


## Before the first App Store release

*Condition:* `app_store_release`

### Needs you (1)

**PLAT-23** · MUST · An app that ships cryptography not provided by Apple's OS goes on the App Store in France only once the French encryption declaration is on file.\
*Why:* Apple requires the declaration for non-OS cryptography in France, as Rust end-to-end encryption is (SEC-11). · *Checked before each release.*


## Before opening to outside contributions

*Condition:* `open_to_contributions`

### Needs you (12)

**REV-03** · SHOULD · Maintainers give a first response to a PR within 3 business days: approve, request changes or hand over. Authors may ping after a week. A reviewer who can't follow up says so. Target review times by change type are published, and actual times are reported each release.\
*Why:* Silence is what drives contributors away; a stated time is a promise they can hold. · *Checked in a periodic audit.*

**GOV-01** · MUST · Significant changes go through a public RFC from the template, in the organization's `rfcs` repository; the RFC number is its pull-request number. Lifecycle: draft; a final comment period of at least 10 days, opened with a proposed disposition; then accepted, rejected or postponed. The author may withdraw at any time, and accepted RFCs become implemented or superseded. An unresolved blocking concern stops the comment period. The decision and its rationale are posted on the RFC, which is never substantially edited afterwards; a later RFC supersedes it and both link each other. Internal, reversible decisions use the light tier: a proposal issue seconded by a maintainer other than the author and left open 7 days, which a blocking concern turns into an RFC. The template requires a stated user problem with a real use case, alternatives including doing nothing and a plugin, how users learn it, an impact section (security, privacy, accessibility, internationalization, data and migration, performance, platforms), and implementation evidence before the comment period. Details: CONTRIBUTING.md.\
*Why:* A timed public comment period and a written rationale protect the project while one person decides. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-05** · MUST · A named human opens every pull request and issue in Kreqo's repositories, writes its description (GOV-14) and answers its review. An agent may push commits to a branch for its human operator. Undisclosed agent activity leads to a ban under the code of conduct.\
*Why:* Contributors and maintainers talk to accountable people, not to agents. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-09** · MUST · While the project is founder-led, the founder decides RFCs and disputes after the public comment period and records the rationale. Area owners decide within their areas. Other decisions use lazy consensus: a proposal stands if no maintainer objects, with reasons, within 72 hours, or within 7 days for anything that changes a public interface. Votes, +1s and popularity never decide features.\
*Why:* A named decider with written reasons beats implied consensus or counting votes. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-10** · MUST · GOVERNANCE.md names the trigger for collective governance, such as three active maintainers or the 1.0 release, whichever comes first. At the trigger, an RFC creates a maintainer council that decides by consent: no outstanding objection after 10 days.\
*Why:* Writing the hand-over trigger down now prevents a founder from holding power by default. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-12** · MUST · README and CONTRIBUTING name the public, archived channels: the issue tracker plus one forum or chat. Proposals and decisions live there, and anything decided in chat or a meeting is written up there. Private channels exist only for security and conduct reports.\
*Why:* Decisions nobody can find later aren't decisions. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-15** · MUST · Maintainers may close, without detailed review, contributions that look like unreviewed AI output or are low-effort or unactionable, linking this rule; repeat cases lead to limits under the code of conduct. Nobody is required to use AI or to review AI-assisted work. Good-first issues are reserved for human newcomers. Suspicion alone is never treated as evidence, and harassing anyone over their use of AI is a conduct violation.\
*Why:* Review time is the scarcest resource, and writing style isn't evidence of AI use. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-18** · SHOULD · Features and large changes start as an issue that states the user problem and a real use case, and an area owner accepts it before a PR is opened. Contributors with three or fewer merged PRs get a maintainer's go-ahead before feature or large refactoring PRs; fixes, docs and translations are always welcome. Details: CONTRIBUTING.md.\
*Why:* Agreeing on the problem first avoids reviewing work nobody wanted. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-19** · SHOULD · Maintainers are invited after sustained review, triage or area work. Areas and working groups (design, docs, translation, accessibility) name their leads, and non-code contributors can hold roles. A triage role can label and close but not merge. Elevated access is granted only after a documented review, listed publicly, and removed after 12 months of inactivity; inactive maintainers become emeritus and can return.\
*Why:* Roles with written entry and exit keep access current and recognize non-code work. · *Checked in a periodic audit.*

**GOV-21** · MUST · CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md names a private reporting address and at least two people who handle reports, one of them outside the founder (an external contact while the project has one maintainer). Reports are acknowledged within 24 hours where possible and within 3 days at most, and decided within 7 days or given a new timeline. Anyone involved or conflicted steps aside. Responses follow the Contributor Covenant 3.0 ladder, with a named appeal route, protection from retaliation and confidential records. An anonymized summary is published yearly from 1.0.\
*Why:* The hard case is a report about the founder, which needs a second contact to be credible. · *Checked in review.*

**LEGAL-17** · SHOULD · CONTRIBUTING states that, by signing off, contributors waive their moral rights of integrity and association in favor of the project and all licensees, as far as the law allows; attribution comes from history and an AUTHORS file. The clause is adopted only after legal review confirms a sign-off can carry a waiver. Details: CONTRIBUTING.md.\
*Why:* Moral rights cannot be assigned, only waived, and integrity claims grow once a company commercializes the commons. · *Checked in review.*

**BIZ-06** · MUST · Community contributions are judged on merit even when they overlap a paid feature. They are never refused or delayed to protect revenue, and such cases are decided in public.\
*Why:* Refusing a contribution to protect revenue is the fork trigger. · *Checked in review.*

### Checked for you (1)

- **GOV-08** · MUST · Contributions are accepted under the unmodified Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1, without a CLA. *(tooling)*

### Rules that change

**GOV-14** becomes: Text written for people (issues, PR titles and descriptions, reviews, RFCs, chat) is written by its human author. AI may translate or proofread, with disclosure, and quoted tool output is marked as such. Unedited AI output is never posted to a person. User documentation drafted with AI ships only after human revision, with disclosure (GOV-03). Branch commit messages are outside this rule, because the squash commit that lands carries the human-written PR title and description (CI-13).

### Reminders

- **LEGAL-01:** Draft the section 7 additional permissions with counsel before the first outside contribution.


## Before a second maintainer joins

*Condition:* `maintainers >= 2`

### Checked for you (1)

- **CI-15** · MUST · A CODEOWNERS file covers every path, including the risk-tier paths (GOV-02). *(tooling)*

### Rules that change

**CI-03** becomes: Every change has a human reviewer other than its author; AI tools never count as reviewers (CI-18). Changes written by an AI agent are reviewed by a maintainer who didn't direct the agent, and risk-tier paths follow CI-15.

**CI-18** becomes: AI review bots run from a separate, clearly labeled bot account, never count as an approval, and block a PR only when a human endorses their comment.

**GOV-02** becomes: The author of a change owns its intent, specification, tests and consequences, and can explain what it does and why, whether or not AI wrote the code. Every change passes CI and human review. Changes to risk-tier paths (`unsafe`, cryptography, data formats and migrations, sync, security-sensitive code, the plugin boundary, the public API of shared crates) get line-level human review; other changes get intent-level review plus the automated gates. Each project lists its risk-tier paths in a machine-readable risk file that the review tooling enforces; once CI-15 applies, that file is CODEOWNERS.


## Before 1.0

*Condition:* `preparing_1_0`

### Needs you (2)

**EXT-04** · SHOULD · The plugin boundary is designed before 1.0, even if plugins ship later.\
*Why:* A boundary added after 1.0 either breaks the public API (REL-01) or exposes internals. · *Checked in review.*

**EXT-05** · MUST · The official plugin directory lists only plugins whose OSI-licensed source builds reproducibly, with CC0 or CC BY/BY-SA assets. It accepts no obfuscated or binary-only code, remote code, self-updating, ads, paywalls, donation prompts or client-side telemetry. Plugins declare named network services, accounts, payments and server-side data use up front, send data only on an explicit user action, and honor the app's global online switch. A human reviews every listing; reported violations get a public fix window, then removal.\
*Why:* A listing is an endorsement; reproducible source and human review are what back it. · *Checked before each release.*

### Checked for you (13)

- **ARCH-16** · SHOULD · Niche features start as plugins or separate crates and move into an app or shared crate only after real use and an ADR. *(AI review)*
- **EXT-01** · MUST · Plugins are sandboxed: no file, network or data access without a permission the user granted. *(AI review)*
- **EXT-02** · MUST · Plugin APIs are versioned like any public interface (REL-01). *(tooling)*
- **EXT-03** · SHOULD · Apps that accept plugins run them as WebAssembly components (WASI 0.3 or later). *(AI review)*
- **EXT-07** · SHOULD · Plugins localize through the suite's localization system and reuse suite strings and translation contexts. *(AI review)*
- **DATA-18** · SHOULD · The last release before a format break can read the new format and save in the old one. *(AI review)*
- **UX-14** · MUST · Users can customize the look through token overrides (density, fonts, accent, including the system accent). *(AI review)*
- **PERF-07** · SHOULD · Idle and standard-scenario energy use is measured each release on a documented setup (at least 10 runs, relative standard deviation at most 5%) and published next to earlier results. *(AI review)*
- **QA-08** · SHOULD · Mutation testing (cargo-mutants) runs on a schedule for core crates. *(tooling)*
- **REL-07** · MUST · Deprecated features live for at least one minor release, with a migration path, before removal. *(AI review)*
- **REL-08** · SHOULD · Apps ship stable, beta and nightly channels. *(AI review)*
- **REL-16** · MUST · Breaking changes to formats, the sync protocol and the plugin API are batched into announced major releases, tracked publicly at least one cycle ahead and approved by RFC with a compatibility section, and each ships an automatic migrator. *(AI review)*
- **CI-20** · SHOULD · One account system spans the forge, forum, translation platform and plugin directory. *(AI review)*


## Before the plugin boundary is designed (EXT-04)

*Condition:* `plugin_design`

### Needs you (1)

**EXT-06** · MUST · Before the plugin boundary is designed (EXT-04), an ADR decides how plugins are distributed and permitted on each Tier 1 platform. That includes iOS, where downloaded code may not change app functionality and every data or permission share with a plugin needs the user's consent.\
*Why:* App Store guidelines 2.5.2 and 4.7 constrain the boundary; a design that ignores them fails store review. · *Checked in review.*\
*Open decision:* Plugin distribution and permissions per Tier 1 platform. Leaning: none yet.


## Before sync ships

*Condition:* `sync`

### Checked for you (1)

- **DATA-10** · MUST · Sync is end-to-end encrypted with keys held only on user devices, and metadata such as file and deck names is in scope. *(AI review)*


## Before end-to-end encrypted sync is called stable

*Condition:* `e2ee_stable`

### Needs you (1)

**SEC-10** · MUST · The independent audit of sync and encryption is published in full, findings are tracked to resolution, and the audit is repeated after any change to the protocol or cryptography. It happens before E2EE sync is called stable, 1.0 at the latest. A security review of each app's security boundary is repeated at least every five years.\
*Why:* A published audit lets users verify the encryption claims instead of trusting them, as Standard Notes and Proton do. · *Checked before each release.*


## Before the first sharing service

*Condition:* `sharing_service`

### Checked for you (1)

- **EXT-08** · SHOULD · Content the organization hosts for sharing (decks, themes, plugins) declares a license, is original or openly licensed, discloses AI generation and third-party network use, and falls under the code of conduct. *(AI review)*


## With the first AI feature

*Condition:* `ai_feature`

### Checked for you (2)

- **AIF-04** · MUST · One suite-wide switch blocks all current and future AI features, with their prompts and promotion, and stays set across updates. *(AI review)*
- **AIF-05** · SHOULD · AI output is labeled as AI-generated and never changes user content without explicit acceptance; generated cards, for example, enter a review queue. *(AI review)*


## Before any telemetry

*Condition:* `telemetry`

### Needs you (1)

**PRIV-13** · MUST · Any telemetry an app ever offers follows the KDE telemetry policy with Syncthing's mechanics: each item answers a written question and stops once answered; no unique device, installation or user IDs; data coarsened at the source, stored without IP addresses, free of user content or hints of it; one ask, no nagging, granular levels, a preview of the exact payload; consent stored per payload-schema version and re-asked when it changes; a setting as prominent as any other, needed by no feature, honoring system-wide settings; organization servers only, over TLS; the field list readable offline in the app; aggregates published; public sign-off by two maintainers other than the author.\
*Why:* KDE's policy and Syncthing's payload preview are the strictest published regimes, and a random install ID still identifies a device. · *Checked in review.*


## Before the first email list

*Condition:* `email_list`

### Needs you (1)

**PRIV-14** · MUST · Email lists are express opt-in only, recording the date, wording and source of each consent. Every message, security notices included, identifies the organization with a contact address and carries a free unsubscribe honored within 10 business days. Addresses are not bought or scraped.\
*Why:* CASL covers any list that might promote something paid, profit motive or not, from the first message. · *Checked in review.*


## Before running a hosted service

*Condition:* `hosted_service`

### Needs you (2)

**PRIV-11** · MUST · Personal-information incidents are logged in a register kept at least 24 months. Affected users and regulators (the OPC, the CAI, EU authorities) are notified when the applicable risk threshold is met, and the response plan is published (SEC-15).\
*Why:* PIPEDA requires a 24-month breach record and notification when a breach poses a real risk of significant harm. · *Checked before each release.*

**PRIV-12** · SHOULD · Hosted services publish how they handle legal requests, and a yearly transparency report as far as the law allows. Both are worded to stay accurate under secrecy duties such as those Bill C-22 would attach to some orders.\
*Why:* Bill C-22 would impose secrecy on some orders, so a report cannot promise to disclose what it may not. · *Checked before each release.*

### Checked for you (2)

- **DATA-15** · MUST · Any account, including a sync account, can be deleted in the app and through a direct web link, with its server-side data and without contacting support. *(AI review)*
- **PRIV-10** · MUST · Organization-run services keep raw logs, IP addresses included, for at most 30 days, and any telemetry for at most 60 days after its last update. *(AI review)*


## Before accepting funds

*Condition:* `accepting_funds`

### Needs you (4)

**GOV-11** · MUST · People who decide for the commons disclose any paid or ownership relationship with Kreqo's company, a sponsor, an employer or a competitor, and recuse themselves where it applies; a conflict can't be waived. Payment never buys merge rights, roadmap priority or changes to this document. Once a decision body has five or more members, at most 40% share an affiliation, the company included.\
*Why:* Open-core projects lose trust when the company's interests decide for the commons. · *Checked in review.*

**GOV-24** · MAY · Project funds may buy devices that contributors need for Tier 1 and screen-reader testing (A11Y-05, PLAT-01), under a published policy.\
*Why:* Testing on real devices is what accessibility and platform rules depend on. · *Checked in review.*

**BIZ-08** · MUST · A public funding policy: sponsors get no decision rights over the roadmap, priorities or this document, and money speeds up planned work but never adds to the plan. Written donation-acceptance criteria list sponsor benefits (logo placement, contacts); sponsorships that may conflict with the principles are discussed publicly with contributors before acceptance. Income is balanced so no single sponsor exceeds a stated share. Money goes only through a fiscal host or the legal entity, never a personal account, and an accountant confirms tax treatment before any money is accepted.\
*Why:* Blender's 2026 patronage reversal shows a sponsor can cost more than it pays. · *Checked in review.*

**BIZ-09** · MUST · A yearly public report gives income by source, spending by category, and paid contributors and grants; funded work programs publish their budget and results; paid contributors publish short, regular work reports.\
*Why:* Public money needs public accounts (Principle 13). · *Checked in a periodic audit.*


## Before commercial use

*Condition:* `commercial`

### Needs you (7)

**A11Y-12** · MUST · Before selling or licensing to public-sector or federally regulated customers, the organization publishes an Accessibility Conformance Report against EN 301 549 for the version sold.\
*Why:* Public-sector and federally regulated buyers require a conformance report under SOR/2025-255. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-07** · MUST · An ADR decides each product's Cyber Resilience Act role: none, manufacturer or steward. As manufacturer, the organization reports under Article 14 from the first commercial release, meets the essential requirements from 11 December 2027 or first placing on the market if later, and mandates an EU authorized representative. As steward, the non-profit adopts a cybersecurity policy. Either way it sets up vulnerability reporting.\
*Why:* Monetizing open source makes the maker a manufacturer; a steward has light duties and no fines. · *Checked before each release.*

**LEGAL-15** · SHOULD · The organization never asserts patents against free software, licenses any patents it holds royalty-free, and joins the Open Invention Network once incorporated.\
*Why:* A patent pledge removes the one claim a permissive license does not already settle. · *Checked in review.*

**LEGAL-16** · MUST · Standard-form terms (sync service, subscriptions, enterprise licenses) are presented in French first, with other languages on no less favorable terms.\
*Why:* The Charter of the French Language requires French-first standard-form contracts from a Quebec establishment. · *Checked before each release.*

**BIZ-02** · MUST · The open/paid boundary is public and versioned before anything is sold. A feature can be paid only if its likely buyer is an organization, not an individual (SSO, central deployment and admin policy, audit logs, SLAs, managed hosting), and paid code lives in separate, clearly labeled repositories. Because apps are GPL and contributions come under the DCO without a CLA, no proprietary license of the apps is ever sold; paid offerings are services, support, hosting, or paid builds of the same code (BIZ-05).\
*Why:* A buyer-based test is the only open-core boundary that doesn't drift. · *Checked in review.*

**BIZ-07** · MUST · The non-profit owns the trademarks, domains, signing keys, store and developer accounts, app IDs and Flathub ownership; until it exists, they are held under LIFE-02 escrow. Code, designs and marks made by any affiliated company belong to the non-profit or are irrevocably licensed to it. The company works under a public, binding agreement with the non-profit that forbids relicensing, and lets the non-profit release under an open license any shared code the company stops developing in the open.\
*Why:* Whoever owns the identities owns the project; the commons must own them. · *Checked in review.*

**BIZ-10** · MUST · An ADR decides the legal form before commercial use or recurring sponsorship. The default is a federal not-for-profit under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act, registered in Quebec, holding the code copyrights, trademarks and domains, with any company operating under license from it. Details: vision document and statutes.\
*Why:* The structure must exist before money or sales, not after a dispute. · *Checked in review.*\
*Open decision:* Legal form. Leaning: A federal not-for-profit registered in Quebec.

### Checked for you (1)

- **BIZ-05** · MUST · The open apps contain no locked features, license-key unlocks, upsell prompts or promotion of proprietary add-ons. *(AI review)*
